text: How Do You Say "Limited Partnership" in German? January 30, 2004 The tanker market is welcoming a relatively new purchasing structure thanks to the German government's tax code. What is known as "KG" is an abbreviation for "Kommanditgesellchaft," which means "limited partnership." The KG scheme has been around for years and has financed a large number of containerships and bulk carriers. In the past few years, KG financings have turned to tankers. The primary benefit of the KG structure is that it allows investors to use tax losses from vessel ownership that can then be used as a write off to reduce personal tax obligations.

How Does It Work - Start with the Money...
In order to purchase a vessel, the KG raises money from private individuals generally through financial intermediaries. This money becomes the "equity" source of capital, which typically covers 40% of the vessel purchase price. Conventional bank loans cover the balance.
The bank loan payments are covered primarily by a time charter and, in the event of a default, the vessel is used as collateral for the balance of the loan. The time charterer could be with a third party but it is usually chartered back to the seller. The seller/time charterer maintains commercial control over the vessel. In some cases, the vessel is time chartered out at a higher rate with the owner locking in a margin. In other cases, the vessel trades on the spot market or is placed into one of the major pools depending on its size. At today's high market rates, the spot market is preferred.
The time charter often runs from 5 to 10 years and is set at a level to cover operating costs, debt repayment obligations, and a return on the equity investment. The time charterer generally has the option to purchase the vessel from the KG at certain points during the time charter period.
Add in Tax Breaks...
The KG, as a German entity, can depreciate the vessel for tax purposes at an accelerated rate. This accelerated depreciation expense is a key component of the investment criteria as the tax losses in the early years are passed to the equity investors. These investors, who are generally high- income individuals, can see a significant reduction in their tax obligations.
The KG, in order to function by the tax code, is obligated to enter into a ship management agreement with a German entity. The German entity can then either operate the vessel through a third party, or in some cases, through a German subsidiary.
Decide on the Tonnage Tax...
At a stipulated point in time, the equity owners must declare whether they desire to be taxed based on the earnings of the vessel or on its tonnage. The latter eliminates income taxes on vessel profits that are no longer shielded by accelerated depreciation.
Thus this is an effective method of enhancing the after tax return to the investors. This will also be reflected in the KG's ability to offer competitive time charter rates. text: Laws in 17 US states enacted during the past four years and expected to be implemented through 2006 require the oil industry to add ethanol, a corn-based substance to gasoline in lieu of methyl tertiary butyl ether or MTBE. The net effect of this change will be increased reliance on imported gasoline this summer and beyond. The federal government is subsidizing what amounts to moonshine-fueled vehicles for 53 cents per gallon of ethanol. That subsidy will cost US taxpayers about $2 billion a year. Critics of this subsidy contend that ethanol actually takes more energy to produce than it creates. The law of unintended consequences would suggest that this subsidy benefits oil companies because it increases the demand for energy! How Does This Affect the Gasoline Chain? The additive has little benefit for coastal refineries in the way of delivery since it is made in the Midwestern Corn Belt and is not transportable by pipeline. Ethanol eagerly absorbs any moisture getting into the pipeline. Instead, ethanol is moved from distilleries in the Midwest to the Gulf coast by railcar and from US Gulf coast marine terminals via chemical carriers to New York, one of the 17 states with an MTBE ban effective Jan. 1st of this year (California is another). The ethanol is sent to blending points from the ports by tank truck where it is added into gasoline at the last minute before going to the filling station. More Volatile than MTBE-blended Gas Ethanol is more volatile than MTBE and releases more photo reactive compounds into the earth's atmosphere that contribute to smog. Gasoline blended with MTBE also contains lighter compounds found at the top of a crude oil barrel. The problem affecting gasoline production in US refineries with regard to ethanol is that these lighter compounds cannot be used with ethanol at all due to the high level of volatility this mixture creates. This reduces the overall volume of gasoline that can be produced in the United States and will push up US reliance on imports of base gasoline. text:
It's a good time to own a ship that needs scrapping. With rates reaching $400 per ton, and in some cases even higher, the industry has never seen such high prices paid for scrap vessels. This increase in scrap prices is being driven by China, which needs steel for reinforcing bar (or rebar) to provide support for the concrete used in infrastructure projects such as buildings and bridges. Secondly, alternative steel is not being produced fast enough as coal and iron ore are also in high demand. And, with tanker earnings still at strong levels, owners of older tonnage want "one more voyage," and need a significant scrap incentive to forego the earnings available on the spot market, thereby reducing available supply. Asset Prices are Up! Four years ago when scrap was $125 LDT, a VLCC of 35,000 tons was worth about $4.4 million. Today that same ship is worth about $14 million. So with considerable foresight (and bravery) a true speculator could have bought four or five old tankers, simply left them at anchor and have seen quite a return. But that would have been a tough one to foresee.
So Why High Scrap Prices? Since the start of 2002, the rising value of rebar (the most common use of scrap steel) has had a very strong influence on scrap prices. Steel prices are going up in response to the enormous pace of economic development taking place in China. China is responsible for a general rise in world commodity prices, not just steel alone. Commodity prices are likely to remain high as long as China keeps expanding at its torrid pace. This pace cannot continue forever, so if an owner is in the mood for scrapping a vessel, maybe this is the time to do it.

It's More Than Just Oil!
The Middle East has always been an important and strategic trading region throughout world history. Today the region remains a critical part of the world economy. In addition to its large consumer base, the region contains significant natural reserves - particularly oil and gas. The world consumes 78 million barrels of oil per day and The Middle East produces about 30% of that total. Giant reserves found in the early 1950s in Saudi Arabia and surrounding nations have rendered the Middle East and oil synonymous in energy parlance. Increasing Russian and West African supplies to Europe and North America have recently shifted some of the Middle East supply focus to the Far East with incremental exports to China and India growing regionally, but the west is an important customer base. In total, the world relies on the Middle East for 20-25% of its daily crude oil imports and with 65% of the world's estimated reserves, it will remain a huge component of future energy requirements.
Causes, Consequences and Tanker Owners The tanker business is a consequence of a cause. The economic well being for tanker owners, in particular VLCC owners, whose aggregate deadweight capacity is about half of the world tanker fleet, is dependent on Middle East exports. Middle East exports are also a consequence of a cause: U.S. and Asian oil import demand. The demand for crude is there, and the good news for owners has always been that the supply is a long way from the market. As shown below again in the form of VLCC spot market activity, during the past three years, most of the Middle East crude has gone to the Far East.

text: What every ship owner knows post the 1973 Middle East oil crisis is that he really never knows. And with VLCC newbuilding prices the highest they've been in nearly 10 years, wild cards such as an oil crisis are decidedly less palatable to the taste. Last year, with record high rates, volatility worked in the owners' favor. But whether rates will meet the expectations of shipowners in the future remains to be seen. Owners looking to build a ship are considering three things: increase in oil demand (the US EIA predicts global demand for oil will rise by 40 million bpd over the next 20 years compared to the current world consumption of 77 million bpd), the development of new trading routes (West Africa to the Far East) and China's demand, so long as it remains. Peering into the future is not easy. While a decent time charter provides a secure income for an owner in the long run, playing the spot market under the present high conditions is likely to be more profitable - but for how long? Looking at the orderbook and measuring growth in annual ton/mile demand against it and the existing fleet is the best benchmark an owner has. Currently, high steel prices and ship demand are causing newbuilding price quotes to skyrocket. The lack of steel in some shipyards of the three major shipbuilding nations is causing newbuildings for 2007 and 2008 to be delayed. Some shipyards are not accepting any more ship orders beyond late 2007 or 2008 delivery because of the lack of berth availability, insecurity stemming from the dollar's weakness, as well as uncertain steel cost. All of this is contributing to higher newbuilding prices. In addition, LNG ships, container ships and bulk carriers are in greater demand which also taxes shipyard space and steel availability. A Sample of Ship Prices In 1999, a VLCC cost around $70 million to build. This month, the newbuilding price for a VLCC is $86 million for a 2007 delivery. Current ship supply/demand is balanced since double-hull ships are not overbuilt and will be needed to meet upcoming environmental regulatory requirements. The fact that yard space is lacking also helps to keep ship supply more predictable. In spite of rates being low, VLCC prices were high from 1995 to 2000, as seen in the graph below.

text: Depending on where your attention is these days, much of the world is preoccupied with war and the economy or the end of popular TV shows. But there has been an intrinsically more interesting story brewing in the popular media during the past few months with analysts, scholars, politicians, and economists beginning to mumble about the world running out of oil. The concept was proposed many years ago and the past two decades have shown that companies were up to the task of finding more oil. But with oil prices at more than $40 per barrel on significantly increased demand, it is a good time to revisit the hypothesis that the world is running out of oil and hence prices are likely to remain above their long-term averages. As shown on the next page, since 1960 the United States has doubled its consumption of crude oil and at 20 million barrels per day, it is still the world's single largest consumer. However, in 1960, the US accounted for more than 45% of worldwide demand. Today it only accounts for about 25% as the growth in Japan and emerging markets in China and India have pushed consumption up to over 80 million barrels per day.

It's not that the world will run out of oil in the short-run, he has said on several occasions, but rather there will not be enough to go around at the current increasing rates of worldwide consumption and hence price increases are inevitable as the world competes for what is ultimately a limited resource. text:
It has been said that what goes up will usually come down. In the case of stock indexes, the measurement of that theory is calculated in numerous factors. For example, Poten's Tanker Index (PTI), started in 1996, is based on weekly- assessed tanker rates for 14 of the most popular trade routes for the principal ship sizes. Since its inception it has been used to measure the health of the tanker market. Another index by Lazard Freres measures the health of stocks of nine large tanker-owning companies. Both indices were set at an index value of 100 for tanker stocks and Worldscale rates in the beginning of 1996. Last week some of those "numerous" variables began to creep into the market. Tanker rates and stocks were strong last year hinging on worldwide increase in demand for crude oil as well as other raw materials. With the slower summer season on the horizon for tankers, what does this mean for tanker stocks? Let's examine the relationship between the two indexes. And the Index Says....
As shown below, there have been considerable periods when the two indices were very close together and where tanker stock prices and tanker rates moved up and down in pretty close unison. In other words a 10% improvement in rates was accompanied by a 10% improvement in tanker stock prices.
The "era of good agreement" between the two indices lasted from January 1996 through September 2000. Then tanker rates increased and tanker stocks decreased and vice versa. What caused this schism? In December 1999, the 25- year-old single-hull ship the Erika broke in two and sank off the coast of Brittany, France, spilling 15,000 tons of heavy grade fuel oil into the ocean. It is likely that the highly-publicized incident caused stockholders to sell their shares in tanker companies, even while tanker owners were still getting good rates for transporting oil (see graph below).

text: Depending on where your attention is these days, much of the world is preoccupied with war and the economy or the end of popular TV shows. But there has been an intrinsically more interesting story brewing in the popular media during the past few months with analysts, scholars, politicians, and economists beginning to mumble about the world running out of oil. The concept was proposed many years ago and the past two decades have shown that companies were up to the task of finding more oil. But with oil prices at more than $40 per barrel on significantly increased demand, it is a good time to revisit the hypothesis that the world is running out of oil and hence prices are likely to remain above their long-term averages. As shown on the next page, since 1960 the United States has doubled its consumption of crude oil and at 20 million barrels per day, it is still the world's single largest consumer. However, in 1960, the US accounted for more than 45% of worldwide demand. Today it only accounts for about 25% as the growth in Japan and emerging markets in China and India have pushed consumption up to over 80 million barrels per day.

text: Post-September 11th, the shipping industry, like many others, came up with its own contingency plan to thwart potential acts of terrorism on ships and terminals and July 1st is the due date for compliance with the provisions. The International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code came into being after the Maritime Safety Committee within the International Maritime Organization (IMO) met with 108 national governments for a year to design the program. In the US, the code was adopted into law as the Maritime Transportation Security Act of 2002. A couple of the more onerous procedures are gathering Declarations of Security from the previous 10 ports that the ship passed through and obtaining an International Ship Security Certificate (ISSC) that says the ship is in compliance with the regulations. The uncertainty is that no one knows what will happen to foreign-flag vessels calling on US ports which are noncompliant with new regulations. Speculation is that the code could be enforced differently in different ports with the Coast Guard taking a number of actions including boarding a vessel more than once, allowing extra time to meet compliance with the regulations, turning the vessel away and, at worst, cutting off trade with the non-complying nations. The last and most severe action would not happen without input from other agencies such as the U.S. Department of State and Marad.

text: While the Coast Guard will be busy implementing these security measures, charterers may incur demurrage charges if a ship is delayed from reaching a port. Various new charter party clauses have been introduced to clarify whether owners or charterers will be responsible for inspection/compliance charges for any delays. The acceptance of such clauses is negotiable between charterers and owners. Depending on the violation, the Coast Guard could allow a ship to wait outside of US waters for an undetermined amount of time to have documentation delivered onto the vessel. Last week, daily demurrage rates were $80,000 for a VLCC; $54,000 for a Suezmax; $35,000 for an Aframax; $23,000 for a Panamax and $20,000 for a Handymax. With crude oil prices at their current levels, these additional costs would probably not be welcome. The responsibilities between owner and charterer are split within the code. The charterer is to provide security officers. Some companies are following the Baltic and International Maritime Council's ISPS clause that holds the charterer responsible for demurrage charges in the event of a delay. Chartering departments of some oil majors will split the demurrage costs with owners, while other owners have refused to incur the charges.

text:
Starting on July 1st and lasting through September 30, 2004, port state control will carry out a concentrated inspection campaign (CIC). The CIC is not limited to the United States, but includes the nations who are signatories to the Paris, Tokyo and Black Sea Memoranda of Understanding (MOU). The Paris MOU includes most of the nations of Europe, the Tokyo MOU includes Australia, Canada, China, Japan and a host of other Asian nations, and the Black Sea MOU which includes Russia, Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania, Georgia and Ukraine. The United States is not a signatory to any of these MOUs, but will participate in the CIC through the U.S. Coast Guard. As background the objectives of the ISPS Code are: 1. Establish an international framework of laws and procedures involving cooperation between contracting (or local) governments, government agencies, local administration and the shipping and port industries to detect/assess security threats and take preventive measures against security incidents affecting ships or port facilities used in international trade.
2. Establish the respective roles and responsibilities of all these parties concerned, at the national and international level, for ensuring maritime security. 3. Ensure the early and efficient collation and exchange of security-related information. 4. A Feeble Attempt to Boost a Wilting Industry Marad has issued an RFP to American shipping companies for up to five clean US-flagged tankers under its Product Carrier Program within the Maritime Security Act of 2003. The first response is due July 2nd. The historical mission of the U.S. government in supporting the maritime interests of the nation was to have a cadre of seafarers and a viable shipbuilding program in place in case of national emergencies. For this reason, U.S. flag vessels had to be built in the United States and manned by U.S. citizens. This case is no different. The MARAD product carriers will be used to carry petroleum products for military supply in case of war or national emergency. Outside of that mission, the ships will be trading in the foreign market and American owners are wondering whether the subsidies offered by the US government will be enough to compete internationally.
The program provides subsidies up to $50 million per vessel to be built in US shipyards. The government contribution is supposed to keep building costs for US shipping companies competitive with international yards. But there are taxes and operation costs to be considered as well. The US government is attempting to address one of those issues by changing the tax structure. Currently, owners pay taxes on profits. A proposal that would place a flat tax on tonnage and reinstitute deferral of income taxes is slowly making its way through Congress. The bill is an amendment to the American Jobs Creation Act, intending that by taxing owners on tonnage rather than earnings, it will lower costs and create a more competitive edge for US-flagged ships and American shipbuilders and seafarers in the foreign market.
The legislation is said to be gaining momentum, though the exact form has not been mentioned. What also has not been in discussion is the cost of a US crew per day to operate a medium-size product carrier compared to a foreign crew. The difference in operating costs could be as much as $2 million for US-flagged ships versus foreign flagged. During the first and second World Wars, the United States embarked on a massive build up of the merchant marine to support military campaigns in Europe and Asia. During World War II, Henry J. Kaiser applied the Ford principle of assembling automobiles to ships. Over 2,700 Liberty ships were built, each capable of carrying over 9,000 tons of cargo. The world record for building a Liberty vessel was less than 10 days from keel laying to launching. The United States could build and fill ships with cargo faster than they were lost.
Several programs were set up to maintain a U.S. flag presence to support the nation in times of national emergencies. One was the long-standing cabotage law, the Jones Act, which restricts the movement of cargoes between U.S. ports to U.S. flag vessels. Jones Act trades have their own unique rate structure that reflects the underlying costs of U.S. flag vessels. Too many U.S. flag vessels in relation to cargoes would cause rates and profit margins to fall, and too few vessels would create small fortunes for their owners. Oil is the most important cargo moving between U.S. ports. The primary trade routes are crude oil from Alaska to U.S. refineries and clean products from the U.S. Gulf to the Northeast. The falloff in Alaskan output created a surplus for U.S. flag crude carriers until in recent years when single hull phase out requirements under OPA'90 trimmed the fleet to a point where ship replacement was necessary. The U.S. Gulf to US East Coast trade was dealt a deathblow in 1980 when President Reagan permitted the exports of U.S. refined products. This gave oil companies a choice of exporting refined products to Mexico and Europe in non-U.S. flag product carriers or in U.S. flag product carriers to the US East Coast. This exposed the protected Jones Act trade to competition from foreign product carriers. To protect U.S. flag tankers in foreign trade, a number of programs were initiated. One was cargo preference for Public Law 480 for grain cargoes to foreign nations. A percentage of these cargoes was reserved for U.S. flag bulk carriers whose rates for carrying the grain reflected their higher capital and operating costs.

Norway's oil workers threatened to strike this past week potentially knocking between 720,000 to 2.5 million barrels per day out of the current exports of 3.2 million bpd. Norway is the world's fourth largest crude oil exporter behind Saudi Arabia, Russia, and Iran. The Norwegian government was successful in ending the week-long strike by negotiating a settlement between employers, which include several oil majors, and workers. But what would have happened if Norway did stop exporting crude oil?
Saudi Arabia stepped up to the plate and said it would make up for Norway's waning exports, should the strike have occurred. But could that have happened and what affect would it have had on the tanker and oil markets?
Saudi Arabia exports 9.8 million bpd with a production capacity estimated to be as high as 12 million bpd. Saudi Arabia could feasibly fill the void of Norway's cessation of production. As seen in the graph on the next page, Saudi Arabia is already producing at historically high levels.

text: Consumption Longer Voyage, More Ships, Higher Rates The upshot of a cessation of exports from Norway would have to be a substitution by Saudi Arabian crude since Russia is producing at maximum capacity and Venezuela and Iran are close to maximum. Such an event would not only strain Saudi Arabia, but also would drain the VLCC fleet capacity and consequently drive rates to extreme highs. VLCCs would have to load in the Arabian Gulf and sail around the Cape of Good Hope instead of Aframaxes making the short run between the Norwegian North Sea terminals and the UKC. Assuming a 75 day round trip, taking into consideration some delays for weather and terminal availability, about 100 VLCCs would be needed per year to ship the Saudi Arabian crude in place of the 2.5 million barrels per day of Norwegian North Sea crude. This represents almost 25% of the existing fleet of 432 vessels, which, to put it mildly, would exert some upward pressure on rates. As 2.5 million bpd would probably consume the entire spare capacity of Saudi Arabia, then one could also look to escalating oil prices to accompany increasing tanker rates. Crude oil futures rose to a 21-year high of $43 dollars per barrel yesterday on the Russian government's announcement that it had curtailed Yukos, the country's largest oil producer, from producing and selling oil. Press reports said the Russian Government would not let the company operate because it owed huge amounts of money in back taxes. The government yesterday told Yukos it could no longer sell its property, which was understood as its oil as well as fixed assets. The Kremlin later clarified the statement and said the company could continue producing oil while its other assets remain frozen. Although crude oil prices fell marginally, they ended today back over $43 per barrel. Investors sense that the problems with Yukos defy such a simple solution. Yukos is one of the main exporters sending half of its 1.8 million bpd production to destinations outside Russia. One of the key drivers of the strength of the tanker market has been the increase in Russian crude exports. If the market were to lose a significant amount of Russian exports, the tanker market would certainly change. For Voyages to Exotic Places Naphtha, unlike other clean petroleum products, has no retail market of any significance. No one buys a truckload to heat his house or a tankful to power his automobile. Until a few years ago, someone in your neighborhood might have bought a few tons at a time to fuel his F-16. But those days have gone. Now, all the fighter jets, even consumer models, burn kerosene. Only refiners, petrochemical companies, and the occasional power station or fertilizer plant want naphtha today. They don't buy their supply at a filling station. They usually get it delivered by ship.
Most of the world's naphtha doesn't trade. Refiners distill it from crude oil and immediately turn it into motor gasoline. But a very large amount remains for other ("merchant") uses. text: The resource-rich South American nation is the world's fifth largest exporter of crude oil, with much of it going to the United States. With about 1.4 million barrels per day shipping to the U.S., Venezuela supplies about 15% of U.S. imports, not including crude oil sent to the Caribbean and refined for the U.S. market. Last year of 2.3 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil produced, 1.1 million bpd were exported to the United States. The US is also a large importer of refined products from Venezuela. Upheaval Again This is not the first time that Venezuelans have tried to remove President Chavez from office. Since he took office, he has faced down two coups in April 2002 and December 2002. Chavez has shown that his politics do not always lend themselves to prime utilization of the nation's resources. In 2003, he fired more than 15,000 oil workers, many of whom were trained to work refinery equipment, from state-owned oil company PdVSA after they organized a strike against him, reducing product exports next to nothing at the beginning of this year. Tanker Rates Rise on Chaos Spot freight rates rise on instability. In the same way Iraq's stop and go oil flow drove rates in the VLCC market up, Venezuela's political situation is cause for increase in WS rates in the Handymax and Aframax markets. Trans-Atlantic shipments ex-UKC have replaced Caribbean voyages for clean products, driving Handymax rates up. Aframax rates have historically increased on top of Handymax rates in the frenzy of trying to fix a ship in an uncertain market. The expectation is that the Aframax market, since that ship size is most used to transport crude oil from South America and the Caribbean to northern points, would suffer if Chavez is overthrown and the interim government cannot manage the nation's oil industry. This of course remains to be seen. In the past, Middle East cargoes have replaced Caribbean crude oil exports. In the meantime, rates this time last year were almost a full 100 WS points lower than they were this week (WS 130 August last year to WS 212 this week) for an Aframax voyage. text: The general public's perception of oil spills is that tankers are a major source of pollution on the high seas, that their record, if anything, is worsening, and that little is being done to correct the situation. The irony and reality is that the greatest oil polluter is nature itself. Restricting our attention to the coastal waters surrounding North America, average annual releases of petroleum were 260,000 tons during the 1990s according to the National Research Council publication Oil in the Sea III: Inputs, Fates, and Effects. Of the 260,000 tons, 160,000 tons were natural petroleum seepages. As an aside, the initial discoveries of oil in western Pennsylvania and in the Baku region of the Caspian Sea were in areas where oil had seeped to the surface of the ground. Oil Creek in Pennsylvania received that name from its oily sheen, which predated the age of oil.

Of the 84,000 tons from this source, 54,000 tons are from land-based river runoff such as individuals dumping used lubricating oils in the local stream. Between 1979 and 1990 the Atlantic Empress , Castillo de Bellver , and the ABT Summer each dumped more than 250,000 tons of crude into the waters yet public perception has been shaped primarily by three relatively smaller oil spills: Exxon Valdez in 1989 of 37,000 tons, Erika in 2000 of 20,000 tons, and the Prestige in 2002 of 77,000 tons. Hurricane Charley made landfall in Florida on Aug. 13 destroying an estimated $15 billion worth of property and homes. text:
We have no place else to look except India and China, both booming economies. Of the two, China is the greater and its consumption of copper, steel, iron ore, coal and other commodities has been a boon to suppliers and its exports and imports of goods have been a boon for container vessel owners. As to oil imports, the IEA has upwardly revised its estimates of China's oil consumption repeatedly. The question is how much of the incremental OPEC production is being consumed and how much is being put away for a rainy day? If inventory accumulation is occurring in China and elsewhere, then when the tanks are full, there is going to be a day of reckoning for those long in oil futures. The problem with this scenario is an apparent lack of sufficient tank capacity to accumulate huge volumes of inventory. Only a few VLCCs have been fixed for floating storage. If China is consuming incremental OPEC production, and if it continues to do so, then we may have crossed over to a world where demand is consuming the entire world's supply of oil. If true, forget about the oil prices falling; rather look forward to rising prices until they reach a level that dampens global oil demand. This will then give supply a chance to catch up with demand putting pressure on oil prices. Economies can cool rapidly if we look at the speed that Southeast Asian economies contracted during the Asian crisis in 1997/98.
Where Do We Go From Here? If crude oil supplies have been tapped out, then there will be limited growth in the number of cargoes regardless of Chinese demand. This could lead to still higher oil prices, which of itself, can begin to cool the global economy. Moreover by the end of 2005, another 40 Vlccs will be delivered, which net of a few scrapings, represent 8% growth of fleet supply. A tapping out of oil supplies, a potential cooling of economic activity in China and elsewhere, and growth in Vlcc supply means continued high rates for a while and then a general retrenchment depending on the timing and degree of any adjustment to the world or to China's economy.

China is not just driving the shipping market to historical highs. Its demand for raw material imports has driven up the prices of oil, steel, and copper to record levels. China has become the world's largest exporter of consumer goods. China is widely blamed for the loss of jobs in the United States through outsourcing of manufacturing activities. But the truth of the matter is that workers around the world involved with consumer goods have been affected by China including Mexico, Jamaica, and nations in Southeast Asia. On the other hand, workers employed in manufacturing capital goods (electricity generators, machinery and equipment) have benefited by China's economic explosion. Economic activity in Germany and Japan has been bolstered by greatly increased capital goods exports to China. U.S. exports to China of steel and equipment are also rising. Let's look at the Asian economic crisis of 1997/98 1 . The first signal that the imposing financial façade of Asia had a weak foundation was the bankruptcy of the Hanbo Steel in Korea in January 1997. In February, Somprasong was the first Thai company to miss its foreign debt payments. In March, a real estate collapse was underway in Thailand with the government reneging on a promise to buy $3.9 1 See website http://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~nroubini/asia/AsiaChronology1.html for a step-by-step chronology of events throughout the crisis.
billion of bad property debt from the nation's banks. In Korea, Sammi Steel failed. At this point, the IMF concluded that the financial crisis had run its course. This was proven wrong soon thereafter when the Malaysian central bank tried to restrict property and stock loans to stem a growing crisis. In May, there was a run on the Thai currency accompanied by the collapse of the nation's largest financing company followed in June by another sixteen financing companies. text: Oil prices are "down" to the high $40's and everyone is breathing a sigh of relief. It might be premature. There are some important things we can think about: § new refineries in India and China have been built for medium to sweet crude; § there is limited spare oil export capacity for medium to sweet crudes; § spare oil export capacity is concentrated in sour crudes; and § refineries that process sour crudes are operating at maximum sustainable capacity. If demand for medium or sweet crudes continues to escalate or if the supply of sweet crude falls such as from cessation of Nigerian exports, prices can climb back to the mid-$50's, or higher. High oil prices adversely affect economic activity. The oil crisis of 1973 set off a global economic retrenchment. As consumers pay more for oil, there is less money to spend on goods. text:
All our professional lives we were taught that handymax tankers are built and make their profits in clean trading. Only those approaching the end of their useful lives trade dirty with worn out coatings whose replacement cost cannot be justified by the market. It was a sign that the grim breaker was nearing. Today it is quite different. Handymaxes can earn over $70,000 per day carrying dirty cargoes out of the Black Sea whereas handymaxes carrying clean cargoes out of the Caribs earn only half that amount. Why Is This So? The answer to this question is congestion in the Dardanelles where transits of large vessels over 200 meters are restricted to daylight hours. With the days getting shorter, northbound transits are down to about 6-8 vessels per day. Smaller vessels can slip in and out while the big boys bide their time at anchor. Of course this means higher shipping costs for charterers of smaller handymaxes, but not after demurrage charges on the big boys are taken into consideration. Moreover a need for immediate delivery of a cargo may toss comparative economics out the window. Current delay expectations northbound are about 6 days (4-5 days in the Dardanelles and 1-2 days in the Bosphorus) with about 5 days southbound. There are 19 tankers in the Dardanelles and 4 tankers in Marmara Sea awaiting permission to make northbound transits. For the southbound transit, there are 15 tankers (3 in the Black Sea and 12 tankers between the Marmara Sea and the Dardanelles) awaiting permission to proceed.
Before 2001 there were very few handymaxes fixed out of the Black Sea and 2002 saw a small step up. Since 2003, the number of spot fixtures has increased significantly, and continues to do so.
